scenes.headline: Serialization & Data Formats
scenes.subtitle: Turning objects into bytes and back
scenes.narration: Serialization is the art of converting in-memory Python objects into bytes that can be stored or sent across a network, and choosing the right format shapes the speed, size, and safety of your pipelines.

scenes.headline: The main options
items: JSON — human-readable, universal, but verbose and untyped
pickle — native Python objects, but unsafe and Python-only
Avro & Parquet — schema-driven binary formats for big data
scenes.narration: JSON is the lingua franca of the web: readable and supported everywhere, though it is bulky and forgets your types. pickle can serialize almost any Python object faithfully, but it is Python-specific and dangerous to load from untrusted sources. For large-scale data engineering, schema-driven binary formats like Avro and Parquet win on size, speed, and the guarantees a schema provides.

scenes.headline: Text vs Binary formats
scenes.narration: Text formats trade efficiency for legibility: you can open them in any editor and any language can parse them, which is invaluable for debugging and interchange. Binary formats give that up in exchange for compact storage, fast parsing, and an embedded schema that enforces structure. Use text at the edges of your system where humans and diverse tools interact, and binary in the high-volume core where performance matters.

scenes.headline: JSON with custom encoding
scenes.narration: json.dumps handles primitives natively but does not know how to serialize a datetime. By passing a default function, you give json a fallback that is called for any unsupported object. Here it converts datetimes into ISO strings and raises a clear TypeError for anything else. This hook is the standard way to teach JSON about your custom types without abandoning the format.

scenes.headline: The danger of pickle
scenes.code:
import pickle

# Safe: your own trusted data
with open("model.pkl", "wb") as f:
    pickle.dump(trained_model, f)

# NEVER do this with untrusted input:
# pickle.load(open(downloaded_file, "rb"))
# Unpickling can execute arbitrary code!
scenes.narration: pickle is wonderfully convenient for persisting your own objects, such as a trained model, in a single call. The critical caveat is that unpickling is not just data loading: a malicious pickle can execute arbitrary code as it is deserialized. That means you must never pickle.load anything that arrived from an untrusted source, and you should prefer safer formats for any data crossing a trust boundary.

scenes.headline: Choosing a format
nodes: Humans or many languages read it?
scenes.narration: Let the audience decide the format. If people or a variety of languages need to read the data, JSON or CSV keeps it accessible. If it is high-volume data flowing between your own systems, Parquet or Avro delivers the compression, speed, and schema enforcement those pipelines demand.

scenes.text: Match the format to the audience: text for interchange, binary with a schema for scale — and never unpickle untrusted data.
scenes.narration: Pick your serialization format by who consumes the data, favoring readable text for interchange and schema-driven binary for scale. And treat pickle from untrusted sources as a security hazard, never a convenience.
